Right. So, the main points are:
1. Core kubernetes does not use this AddressType value; the EndpointSlice controller has never generated slices with this type, and kube-proxy has always ignored slices with this type.
2. The exact meaning/intent of this AddressType was never defined, and different third party components have used it in different and potentially incompatible ways.
3. The obvious use cases for this type run into the same problems as https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/97076 and there is no way to address that using only the existing EndpointSlice and Service fields. Using Gateway rather than Service+AddressTypeFQDN EndpointSlice is probably a better approach.

Of which, the second is most relevant to the API documentation if we want to avoid being too verbose.

issue_context.title: no defined semantics for EndpointSlices of type "FQDN"
issue_context.body:
The API docs (and the end-user docs) state that "FQDN" is a valid value for EndpointSlice.AddressType, but nothing explains what the expected semantics of an FQDN slice are. And in fact, the expected semantics seem to be "[it gets ignored](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.26.0-rc.0/pkg/proxy/endpoints_test.go#L1590)".

We should document what FQDN slices are for, and if the answer is (and always will be) "nothing" then we should mark that value deprecated.

/assign @robscott 
/kind bug
/kind documentation
/sig network
/priority backlog
comments:
> . And in fact, the expected semantics seem to be "[it gets ignored](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.26.0-rc.0/pkg/proxy/endpoints_test.go#L1590)".

that is kube-proxy but slices can be consumed by others.

However, I've tried to find the motivation or some use cases but I couldn't find them https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/84091

So this came out of an OpenShift bug, where a customer was expecting FQDN EndpointSlices to work basically like ExternalName services, except being able to specify multiple remote endpoints. But CoreDNS doesn't implement that, and I don't see any way that it _could_ implement that, because you can't have multiple CNAMEs attached to the same service DNS name. It seems like the only thing that would be able to handle FQDN slices in a useful way would be an L7 proxy?
xref https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/105172

> I don't see any way that it could implement that, because you can't have multiple CNAMEs attached to the same service DNS name. 

I think any implementation would have to involve "flattening" the endpoint FQDNS. e.g.

For a type A query of `example.default.svc.cluster.local.`

The following answer would be illegal in DNS, since there are two CNAMEs with the same name.
```
example.default.svc.cluster.local. CNAME fqdn1.example.com.
example.default.svc.cluster.local. CNAME fqdn2.example.com.
fqdn1.example.com. A  10.0.0.1
fqdn2.example.com. A 10.0.0.2
```
so instead the answer could be flattened to ...
```
example.default.svc.cluster.local. A  10.0.0.1
example.default.svc.cluster.local. A 10.0.0.2
```

This would be like treating the FQDN endpoints as ALIASes.  ALIAS afaik not being an official DNS spec concept, but implemented by various DNS servers more or less as an "invisible" CNAME.

> so instead the answer could be flattened to ...

Ah, true. You can't really resolve the FQDNs to IPs _ahead of time_ and have `example.default.svc.cluster.local` resolve to that list of IPs (this runs into all the same problems as attempting to do FQDN NetworkPolicies), but I suppose CoreDNS could implement it by looking up the FQDNs _at the point when someone tries to resolve `example.default.svc.cluster.local`_ and returning the aggregated list of results.
Could the cluster DNS service publish `SVCB` records rather than `CNAME`s?
ISTR we left this in as a nod towards being more general-purpose, but I can't honestlrecall why it was a good idea.

Agree with @thockin here. This came from the idea that EndpointSlices could be used by different applications for entirely independent purposes, published and consumed by custom implementations. In retrospect I don't think we had sufficiently clear use cases for this, and I don't know of any implementations that make use of this feature today.

What if two applications each decided to use `addressType: FQDN` but interpreted it in incompatible ways?

I don't think EndpointSlice is currently designed correctly to be extensible. (eg, `addressType` must be a registered type, so you're pretty limited in what sorts of "independent purposes" you could use EndpointSlices for)

> We should document what FQDN slices are for, and if the answer is (and always will be) "nothing" then we should mark that value deprecated.

We could also mark it as “reserved” (and even warn if it's used, until whatever release where we start using it in earnest).

Agree - we should mark it deprecated and return an API warning when it is used.  Seems like an easy one for a newish contrib to jump on!

/help-wanted
/triage accepted

I think we should rollback this deprecation - or maybe scope the use of FQDN type to only having a single entry.

Knative was planning on making use of the FQDN type to work around restrictions with Service type=ExternalName

The K8s CVE-2021-25740 mentions https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/103675

> A similar attack is possible using Ingress implementations that support forwarding to ExternalName Services. This can be used to forward to Services in other namespaces or, in some cases, sensitive endpoints within the Ingress implementation. If you are using the Ingress API, we recommend confirming that the implementation you’re using either does not support forwarding to ExternalName Services or supports disabling the functionality.

This was possible with Contour and hence they issued a CVE - https://github.com/projectcontour/contour/security/advisories/GHSA-5ph6-qq5x-7jwc restricting the feature.

With ingresses dropping support for ExternalName we were planning on [migrating](https://github.com/knative/serving/issues/11821) to using EndpointSlices with FQDN. The reasoning being is users don't interact with EndpointSlices and operators can use RBAC rules to limit their creation/modification - but allow the Knative control plane to do so.

Also an observation I noticed is that ingress implementations sorta ignored FQDN because when it became stable in K8s 1.21 it didn't actually work/did anything. It was only until CoreDNS 1.8.4 added support (which kubeadm used for K8s 1.22)  would FQDN act like a CNAME record.

I was also hoping ingress implementations (via the Gateway API) support these types of Services variants - by expanding their conformance tests - https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/issues/1718

> I was also hoping ingress implementations (via the Gateway API) support these types of Services variants - by expanding their conformance tests - [kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api#1718](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/issues/1718)

/cc @robscott

>With ingresses dropping support for ExternalName we were planning on https://github.com/knative/serving/issues/11821 to using EndpointSlices with FQDN. The reasoning being is users don't interact with EndpointSlices and operators can use RBAC rules to limit their creation/modification - but allow the Knative control plane to do so.

This does feel marginally safer, but I'm still not sure how safe it would be. Can you explain some of the specific use case(s) for FQDN addresses?

Knative creates K8s services of type external name which point to a cluster local proxy (typically the proxies service dns name - istio-ingressgateway.istio-system.svc.cluster.local). This allows us to perform L7 type routing within a cluster without a mesh.

> I think we should rollback this deprecation - or maybe scope the use of FQDN type to only having a single entry.

If there are use cases for new EndpointSlice AddressTypes, we could add them. (This would presumably require a KEP.) The problem is that there was no definition of what the existing FQDN type was supposed to mean.

But OTOH, do you actually need to be using `discoveryv1.EndpointSlice`? The slices you want aren't going to be automatically created by the EndpointSlice controller anyway... so why not just make a CRD type for the feature you want?

> If there are use cases for new EndpointSlice AddressTypes, we could add them. (This would presumably require a KEP.) The problem is that there was no definition of what the existing FQDN type was supposed to mean.

Why not backfill the use cases based on empirical usage - generally it seems like FQDN is being used to introduce CNAME records into Kubernetes's DNS services.

ie. using a kind cluster 1.22+
```yaml
apiVersion: discovery.k8s.io/v1
kind: EndpointSlice
metadata:
  name: helloworld
  labels:
    kubernetes.io/service-name: helloworld
addressType: FQDN
ports:
- name: http
  port: 80
  protocol: TCP
endpoints:
  - addresses:
      - "google.com"
    conditions:
      ready: true
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: helloworld
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  ports:
    - name: http
      protocol: TCP
      port: 80
```
```sh
$ kubectl run -ti --restart=Never --rm --image registry.k8s.io/e2e-test-images/jessie-dnsutils:1.3 dnsutils --  nslookup helloworld
Server:		10.96.0.10
Address:	10.96.0.10#53

helloworld.default.svc.cluster.local	canonical name = google.com.
Name:	google.com
Address: 142.251.33.174

pod "dnsutils" deleted
```

Here's an example of a downstream usage in practice - https://github.com/vmware-tanzu/cross-cluster-connectivity/issues/96

> But OTOH, do you actually need to be using discoveryv1.EndpointSlice? The slices you want aren't going to be automatically created by the EndpointSlice controller anyway... so why not just make a CRD type for the feature you want?

Unless I'm missing something - I don't see an alternative to EndpointSlices that let me provide DNS records to the cluster. I don't think creating a CRD is going to help here.

> generally it seems like FQDN is being used to introduce CNAME records into Kubernetes's DNS services.

see @chrisohaver comment in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/114210#issuecomment-1337646747

> The following answer would be illegal in DNS, since there are two CNAMEs with the same name.

However, it seems that it works in CoreDNS with one record, @chrisohaver any idea how this can work ? I can't see you process those types on CoreDNS
https://github.com/coredns/coredns/blob/915b74f2232573746bcc76e1e987775b076a9ef4/plugin/kubernetes/object/endpoint.go#L106
I'm wary of seeing CNAME as a big limitation, because we have records like SVCB likely to come available as standards. And we already have SRV.

So. This is a bit embarrassing. I’ve been following this and scratching my head because I don’t remember this being a feature of CoreDNS. I haven’t had time to confirm, but I think the CoreDNS behavior is  an unintentional result of how the endpointslice is passed to the “backend” to be rendered to a dns record. The backend renders any non-ip record value as a CNAME.

> generally it seems like FQDN is being used to introduce CNAME records into Kubernetes's DNS services

This seems more like a bug than an intentional feature.  We have a supported way of introducing a CNAME record - `Service.spec.type: ExternalName`.  We should not add another equivalent-but-different mechanism.

>> With ingresses dropping support for ExternalName we were planning on knative/serving#11821 to using EndpointSlices with FQDN. The reasoning being is users don't interact with EndpointSlices and operators can use RBAC rules to limit their creation/modification - but allow the Knative control plane to do so.
>
> This does feel marginally safer, but I'm still not sure how safe it would be. 

My thoughts exactly.  Epsilon safer than a literal CVE is not "safe".

> Knative creates K8s services of type external name which point to a cluster local proxy (typically the proxies service dns name - istio-ingressgateway.istio-system.svc.cluster.local). This allows us to perform L7 type routing within a cluster without a mesh.

And this works, right?  As long as you don't try to create an Ingress.

Let's recall what that CVE was about - it was about not letting user B expose user A's workloads to user C (canonical example of C being "the internet"). 

Thinking out loud: 

@robscott this kind of feels like a job for ReferenceGrant, doesn't it?

If one were to drop a refgrant into namespace `istio-system`, expressing "allow access to Service istio-ingressgateway from namespace *", it seems clearer that the controller should allow it.  But actually, wait.  That doesn't distinguish between internal and external use, and once you have access to the proxy, I guess it uses hostname routing?

So could I do this:

User A has a service X intended only for internal traffic, ExternalName = the cluster proxy.
User B creates a service Y, ExternalName = the cluster proxy
User B gives service Y an internet-facing Ingress, which gets IP 1.2.3.4
User C accesses 1.2.3.4 with the hostname header set to "x.a.svc.cluster.local" 

User B has done exactly what that CVE tried to prevent.

Changing ExternalName to FQDN EPSlice limits this only to users who can write EPSlices, which is a small consolation.  Fundamentally you have a shared proxy, whose routing instructions are in the attacker's hands (hostname).  That just can't work, unless the routing is taken out of the attacker's control (e.g. destination IP or port).

Please forgive me if I am making some incorrect leap in logic.

> This seems more like a bug than an intentional feature. 

Your bug is my feature ;)

> And this works, right? As long as you don't try to create an Ingress.

Yup it works but _now_ it depends on the ingress implementation and their posture towards Service type=ExternalName.

> My thoughts exactly. Epsilon safer than a literal CVE is not "safe". ... Changing ExternalName to FQDN EPSlice limits this only to users who can write EPSlices, which is a small consolation.

I think you're on point where users don't create Endpoint[Slice]s and operators can easily create RBAC rules to prevent them. Since the creation of EndpointSlice type=FQDN can be limited to control planes (ie. Knative) I hope ingress implementations feel confident routing to these types of Services by default.

> Please forgive me if I am making some incorrect leap in logic.

Your example doesn't really apply because Knative has a common use case where people create internal Knative Services and then expose a few them to the internet using a DomainMapping feature.  But we have complimentary resources for the operator to limit _who_ can create _what_ mappings.

For this to work we need affordances that Ingress implementations trust.

> You're example doesn't really apply because Knative has a common use case where people create internal Knative Services and then expose a few them to the internet using a DomainMapping feature. But we have complimentary resources for the operator to limit who can create what mappings.

Once traffic arrives at the proxy, how does the proxy decide which backend service to route to?

> Once traffic arrives at the proxy, how does the proxy decide which backend service to route to?

There are logically two proxies - an external one and an internal one. The external one would look at the host of the request - `foo.com` and then send that traffic to the desired backend - `some-revision.default.cluster.local` while rewriting the host. I was a bit too terse [earlier](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/114210#issuecomment-1447488637) so let me expand on DomainMapping a bit.

When you create an public `ksvc` the external URL is created from a template defined by the operator. Typically the template is setup to prevent collisions - ie. `{ksvc-name}.{namespace}.example.com`. DomainMapping let's users bring their own vanity domain - ie. `k8s.gcr.io`. But first the operator needs to authorize a namespace the ability to use a certain domain using a `DomainClaim`. Only once that's created can a user create a `DomainMapping` pointing to their `ksvc`. The way this is accomplish in our network programming is forwarding traffic for `k8s.gcr.io`(external proxy) to the `ksvc` internal URL `(ksvc-name}.{namespace}.svc.cluster.local` and performing a host-rewrite.  `(ksvc-name}.{namespace}.svc.cluster.local` points to the internal proxy via ExternalName/CNAME.

DomainMapping treats the target's as opaque. It's not documented but you can point them to any Kubernetes Service or some thing that conforms to a Knative 'Addressable' duck type (ie. resources that have a `status.address.url` property). Because we treat targets as opaque we don't do any special handling for our own types. Even if we did have special handling there's a few edge cases that would still require forwarding to an internal `svc` - ie. users are creating private `ksvc`s and using DomainMapping to expose a subset of them with vanity domains.

So, the problem here arises from two things:
- there are lots of places where you want to use a relatively-opaque hostname to direct somewhere _outside_ the cluster
- there are some, _limited_ use cases where it's good to be able to use a hostname to direct traffic inside a cluster, _using other ways to manage the security risks inherent in doing so_.

I think that it all comes down to treating the hostname field as opaque. I _think_ that we could make large swaths of at least my concern about all these hostname fields that control traffic flow go away, _purely using API constructs_ using some rules that looked like this:
- ReferenceGrant is available in the cluster
- Any field that uses a hostname for forwarding traffic _must_ be parsed and checked for things that look like `<service>.<namespace>.svc.<cluster-domain>`, and if that pattern is matched, they must be validated by checking that `<service>` in `<namespace>` has a ReferenceGrant allowing the traffic.
- For things that aren't services inside the cluster, knock yourself out.

Of course, this really moves the problem one layer out, in that it means that an attacker with access to a running pod inside the cluster can:
- Find the name and namespace of some service they shouldn't have access to
- Look up the IP associated with `service.namespace.svc.cluster.local`, call it `1.2.3.4`
- Create an external hostname that resolves to `1.2.3.4`
- Use that to get a confused deputy (like an Ingress or Gateway API controller proxy) to forward traffic to that service for you.

(This is why the Gateway API recommendations for ExternalName services use such strong language, because it's reasonably likely that a motivated attacker can fool whatever allowlist mechanisms an implementation puts in place).

The only way to definitely mitigate this problem is to have something that implements network policy, _and, more importantly_, a full set of network policies that only allow access to services from what they're supposed to.
